is_name_purposeful.instructions: This unit is a binding. Does every identifier's name in this unit state what it does or holds, so a reader can infer its purpose from the name alone?

criteria.true: Every identifier's name in this code states what it does or holds: a reader can infer the thing's purpose from the name alone, without reading the surrounding code. Casing and convention style are not part of this judgment.
criteria.false: At least one name reveals implementation instead of purpose (naming how it works, not what it is for), is a bare generic word that could label anything (data, handler, util, temp), or misleads by promising behavior or a kind the thing does not have.

is_naming_convention_consistent.instructions: This unit is a binding. Do identifiers of the same kind in this unit follow a single casing convention?

criteria.true: Identifiers of the same kind follow one casing convention - functions and variables in camelCase, types and classes in PascalCase, module-level constants in SCREAMING_SNAKE - or whichever single form the surrounding code has already established for that kind.
criteria.false: Two different casing forms appear for the same kind within the change or module (getUserData beside fetch_user_data for two functions, OrderItem beside order_item for two types), forcing a reader to learn two shapes for one kind. Different kinds may use different conventions, and word choice or name quality are not casing failures.

is_comment_narration.instructions: This unit is a binding. Does any comment in this unit merely restate what the code in this unit already says, so that removing it loses nothing a reader could not get from the code itself?

criteria.true: At least one comment merely narrates the code: it restates what the code already says - translating statements into prose, echoing the identifier's own name, or annotating the obvious (an increment, an assignment, a return) - so removing it loses nothing a reader could not get from the code itself.
criteria.false: Every comment here says something the code cannot: it states why the code exists, records a constraint, or flags a non-obvious trap.

is_comment_patching_readability.instructions: This unit is a binding. Does any comment here patch code that should read itself, instead of the code being made readable?

criteria.true: At least one comment exists to explain code that should read itself - patching dense expressions, tangled control flow, or misleading names with prose instead of the code being made readable. This is a code smell: the fix is rewriting the code, and the comment makes the confusion livable so the rewrite never happens.
criteria.false: Every comment earns its place by carrying what code cannot: rationale, constraints, or external contracts. Comments that add what code cannot carry are not readability patches, even when the surrounding code is also hard to read.

will_comment_drift.instructions: This unit is a binding. Does any comment pin specific artifacts by name such that renaming or removing them silently invalidates the comment?

criteria.true: At least one comment pins specific artifacts by name - files, functions, parameters, constants, types, paths - such that renaming or removing that artifact silently invalidates the comment while the code keeps working. The claim is coupling between the comment's wording and identifiers, not comments already wrong today.
criteria.false: No comment here is coupled to specific artifacts by name: every comment describes behavior, rationale, or constraints without pinning identifiers, so renaming or removing code can never silently invalidate it.

is_cognitively_complex.instructions: This unit is a binding. How much EFFORT does a reader need to follow this code's logic - effort caused by structure the author chose, not by the problem itself? Ignore length alone: a long linear unit with one job reads as easy. Ignore inherent complexity: cases the data or the domain genuinely force are not this failure. Judge how hard the code's own structure makes it to read top-to-bottom.
criteria: Easy: the logic reads top-to-bottom. A single pass suffices. Any difficulty present is inherent to the problem, not to the structure.

Moderate: the reader must pause once or twice - hold a small amount of state across a few lines, or re-check an outer condition - but the structure is otherwise linear and the full flow is recoverable by re-reading one or two spots.

Hard: following the code requires actively reconstructing its flow - a stack of nested conditions to track, several unrelated concerns fused into one unit, state held across many lines, or an order that forces jumps instead of top-to-bottom reading. The structural difficulty could be removed without changing what the code does.

is_readable.instructions: This unit is a binding. How easy is `source` to read at the identifier/structure level? Do not score algorithmic hardness. Do not score comments here.
criteria: Names, structure, and types make the story obvious.
Mostly clear; a few opaque names or a slightly awkward shape.
Reader must reconstruct intent from implementation details.
Dense, misleading names, or structure that fights the problem.
